claims.text: Functional decline is often caught too late.
claims.poster_quote: Functional decline is often caught too late.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Functional decline in older adults is typically recognized only after falls or observable gait impairment, closing the window for prevention.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that functional decline is often recognized too late, after observable impairment or a fall event. (Abstract, Introduction)

claims.text: Trajectory matters more than single lab values.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory matters more than single lab values.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The central insight motivating this work is that the trajectory of a biomarker may carry more predictive information than any single value.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that trajectory carries more predictive information than single lab values. (Introduction)

claims.text: We use 12 routine biomarkers to predict decline pre-clinically via EHRs.
claims.poster_quote: We use 12 routine biomarkers to predict decline pre-clinically via EHRs.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Using the All of Us Research Program (N = 297,861; 11.1% cases), we derived trajectory features (slope, variability, delta, mean) for twelve biomarkers over a three-year pre-index window.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that 12 routine biomarkers were used to predict functional decline pre-clinically via EHRs. (Abstract)

claims.text: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5.
claims.poster_quote: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5 — existing tools miss this.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that has been stable for three years represents a fundamentally different risk than one that declined from 13.5 g/dL over the same period.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5. (Introduction)

claims.text: Existing tools miss the risk signaled by a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years.
claims.poster_quote: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years signals higher risk than a stable 11.5 — existing tools miss this.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that has been stable for three years represents a fundamentally different risk than one that declined from 13.5 g/dL over the same period. Yet, both appear identical at a single timepoint.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that existing tools miss the risk signaled by a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL that declined from 13.5 over 3 years. (Introduction)

claims.text: Trajectory features beat static summaries with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features beat static summaries: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: LightGBM models incorporating trajectories significantly outperformed static laboratory summaries (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755; DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that trajectory features outperform static summaries with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755. (Abstract, Results)

claims.text: Trajectory features beat static summaries with AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features beat static summaries: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755. AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory features reached 0.797 (0.794–0.800), a significant gain over baseline (∆AUC = 0.042; DeLong p < 0.001). Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that trajectory features outperform static summaries with AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304. (Results, Table 1)

claims.text: Figure 2 shows 25% relative gain in precision-recall.
claims.poster_quote: Figure 2 shows 25% relative gain in precision-recall.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that there is a 25% relative gain in precision-recall. (Results)

claims.text: Trajectory features predict decline better with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features predict decline better: AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: LightGBM models incorporating trajectories significantly outperformed static laboratory summaries (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755; DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that trajectory features predict decline better with AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755. (Abstract, Results)

claims.text: The model uses only existing labs, enabling passive, scalable early detection in any EHR.
claims.poster_quote: Uses only existing labs — enabling passive, scalable early detection in any EHR.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Because the model uses only measurements already ordered in routine care, it supports passive, zero-burden EHR integration for early detection of pre-clinical functional decline.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the model uses only existing labs, enabling passive, scalable early detection in any EHR. (Abstract, Discussion)

claims.text: Independent trajectory signal achieves AUROC 0.727 beyond demographics.
claims.poster_quote: Independent trajectory signal beyond demographics (AUROC 0.727), and model retains strong performance without utilization proxies (AUROC 0.789), supporting equitable deployment.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A 1:1 age- and sex-matched analysis confirmed an independent trajectory signal (AUROC 0.727 vs. demographics-only 0.680).
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that independent trajectory signal achieves AUROC 0.727 beyond demographics. (Abstract, Results)

claims.text: The model retains strong performance without utilization proxies with AUROC 0.789.
claims.poster_quote: Independent trajectory signal beyond demographics (AUROC 0.727), and model retains strong performance without utilization proxies (AUROC 0.789), supporting equitable deployment.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Removing count features yielded AUROC 0.789 (0.786–0.791), a reduction of 0.009 (DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the model retains strong performance without utilization proxies with AUROC 0.789. (Results)

claims.text: The study analyzed 297,861 All of Us participants aged 50–125.
claims.poster_quote: We analyzed 297,861 All of Us participants aged 50–125.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The primary modeling cohort contained 297,861 participants (33,088 cases, 11.1%). Mean age at index was 50.6 years (SD = 16.8).
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states the study analyzed 297,861 participants aged 50–125. (Results)

claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the study used 12 biomarkers over 3 years. (Abstract)

claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the study evaluated models with LightGBM, XGBoost, RF, and LR. (Methods)

claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that cases were defined by ICD-10 codes, including R26.2. (Methods)

claims.text: Controls were assigned pseudo-index dates to avoid immortal time bias.

claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Controls were participants with laboratory data and no qualifying mobility decline diagnosis. A pseudo-index date was assigned by sampling uniformly at random within each control’s laboratory observation window (first to last measurement). This design preserves natural measurement history while preventing immortal time bias.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that controls were assigned pseudo-index dates to avoid immortal time bias. (Methods)

claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: All models were trained with 5-fold stratified cross-validation; out-of-fold (OOF) predictions across all folds were aggregated for unbiased evaluation. SHAP TreeExplainer values were computed on a held-out 20% test set (n = 5,000) to prevent training-data leakage.
